text: For a long time, most scientists believed the continents had always been where they are. In 1912, a German scientist named Alfred Wegener argued that they had once been joined and had slowly drifted apart. He pointed to coastlines that fit like puzzle pieces, matching rocks, and identical fossils on lands now separated by oceans.

Most [[geologist|geologists]] rejected the idea, because nobody could say what force could push a continent. The answer came from the bottom of the sea. In the 1950s and 1960s, scientists mapped a long mountain range down the middle of the Atlantic and found that new sea floor was forming there and spreading outwards.
By the late 1960s, the evidence had become a theory called [[plate|plate]] tectonics. Today, satellites measure the continents moving a few centimetres every year.

st.prompt: Why did most scientists reject Alfred Wegener's idea of drifting continents for so long?

options.t: He couldn't explain what force moved them
His maps showed the coastlines didn't fit
No fossils had been found on two continents

st.reveal: Wegener had strong clues, from matching coastlines to matching fossils. What he lacked was a believable engine. Only when scientists studied the sea floor in the 1950s and 1960s did they find how new crust forms and spreads.

sec.h: The puzzle that didn't go away
sec.t:
People noticed the fit of the coastlines as soon as there were good maps. In 1596, the Flemish mapmaker Abraham Ortelius suggested that the Americas had been torn away from Europe and Africa.

Wegener collected far more than shapes. The [[fossil|fossil]] [[reptile|reptile]] Mesosaurus lived in shallow inland waters and couldn't have crossed an ocean, yet it turns up in Brazil and in South Africa. Leaves of an ancient plant called Glossopteris appear in India, Africa, South America, Australia and even Antarctica. Rocks in hot, [[tropical|tropical]] India carried scratches left by glaciers. To Wegener, it all made sense if these lands had once formed one giant continent, which he called [[@pangaea|Pangaea]].

sec.h: A crack in the middle of the ocean
sec.t:
After the Second World War, ships used echo sounders to map the sea floor. In the 1950s, the American scientist Marie Tharp, working with Bruce Heezen, plotted the soundings by hand. She found a deep valley running along the top of the [[@ocean-floor-maps|Mid-Atlantic Ridge]], where the sea floor seemed to be splitting.

Then came the stripes. Rocks record the direction of Earth's magnetic field when they cool, and that field flips every so often. Scientists found matching stripes of flipped and unflipped rock on both sides of the ridge, like a barcode printed in mirror image. New crust was forming at the ridge and slowly moving away on both sides.

Here, at last, was Wegener's missing engine. Hot rock deep in the [[mantle|mantle]] flows slowly, carrying the plates with it.

Today, [[@gps-how|GPS]] stations bolted to rock show the plates moving in real time. The Atlantic widens by about 2.5 cm a year, roughly as fast as your fingernails grow. India is still pushing north into Asia, which is why the [[@himalaya-form|Himalayas]] are still rising and the region has strong earthquakes.

Wegener's name is now on a crater on the Moon, a crater on Mars and a research institute in Germany that studies the polar ice where he died.

text: The biggest creature in the sea, and probably the biggest animal ever to live, is the [[@blue-whale|blue whale]]. It can grow to about 30 metres long, as long as three school buses, and weigh more than 150 tonnes. Its heart alone weighs about as much as two grown men.

The biggest fish is the whale shark, which usually reaches about 12 metres. The heaviest animal without a backbone is the colossal squid. And if you count length, some strange, stringy animals are even longer than a blue whale.

Seals and dolphins

st.reveal: Whale sharks are gentle filter feeders. They swim with their huge mouths open, straining plankton, fish eggs and tiny fish out of the water. Divers can swim alongside them safely.

sec.t:
Whale sharks are spotted like a starry night sky. Each pattern is unique, so scientists identify individuals from photos, a bit like fingerprints. They are [[filter-feeder|filter feeders]] and harmless to people.

Every year, many whale sharks visit the coast of Gujarat. Fishermen once caught them in large numbers. In 2001 India made the whale shark the first fish to get the strongest legal protection, and Gujarat's fishing villages now help rescue sharks tangled in nets.

The colossal squid lives in icy waters near Antarctica. The heaviest one ever caught, in 2007, weighed about 495 kilograms. It has the biggest eyes of any known animal, each about the size of a football. In 2025 scientists filmed a young colossal squid alive in the deep sea for the first time.

The giant squid is longer and slimmer, reaching perhaps 12 metres including its long feeding [[tentacle|tentacles]]. Sperm whales, the biggest animals with teeth, plunge into the dark to hunt them, and some carry round scars from squid suckers.

Water holds up a heavy body, so bones don't have to carry all the weight. That's why a whale stranded on a beach is in danger even while it can still breathe: out of water, its own weight presses on its lungs. Cold seas also suit big bodies, because a large animal loses heat more slowly than a small one.

Food matters too. [[fossil|Fossils]] suggest the biggest whales grew so huge only in the last few million years, as ocean currents began piling krill into rich patches. A giant mouth can scoop up a whole swarm at once, and a giant body can store fat for long trips between feeding grounds.

Giants have one weakness. They breed slowly, and a blue whale mother usually has a single calf every two or three years. That's why whaling in the 1900s brought them close to disappearing.

Length is a stranger contest. A lion's mane jellyfish washed up in Massachusetts in 1870 had tentacles about 37 metres long. In 2020 a research ship filmed a deep-sea siphonophore off Western Australia coiled in a spiral. Scientists estimated its outer ring alone was about 47 metres long. A siphonophore isn't one animal but a colony of many tiny linked ones working as a team.

For sheer weight among bony fish, the record goes to a giant sunfish found dead near the Azores in 2021, which weighed 2,744 kilograms. And the strangest part? Millions of years ago, the seas held a shark so big that its teeth were as large as your hand, the mighty [[@megalodon|megalodon]].

text: The salt in the sea comes mostly from rocks on land. Rain is very slightly acidic, because it picks up a little [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]] from the air. As it falls on rocks and soaks through soil, it slowly [[dissolve|dissolves]] tiny amounts of minerals. Rivers carry these dissolved minerals down to the sea.

When seawater evaporates in the Sun, the water rises into the sky as vapour, but the salt stays behind. That water falls again as rain, and the cycle repeats, as you can read in [[@water-cycle|the water cycle]]. Over hundreds of millions of years, the salt has built up. Today, every litre of seawater holds about 35 g of salt, roughly six teaspoons.

st.prompt: Rivers carry salt into the sea all the time. So why don't rivers taste salty?

options.t: They carry only a tiny amount, and their water keeps flowing away
River fish eat up the salt
River salt sinks into the mud

st.reveal: River water does carry dissolved salts, but far too little to taste. The water keeps moving on to the sea and is replaced by fresh rain. In the sea, water leaves only by evaporating, and the salt stays behind, building up over millions of years.

myth: If you are stranded at sea, drinking seawater will keep you alive.

Seawater has more salt than your kidneys can handle. To get rid of it, your body has to use up even more water than you drank, so seawater makes thirst worse. Sailors and lifeboats carry fresh water for this reason.

sec.t:
Rivers are not the only source. Along the ocean floor, there are cracks where seawater seeps deep into hot rock. There it picks up minerals and gushes back out of hot springs called hydrothermal vents. Undersea [[@volcano|volcanoes]] add minerals too.

Most of the sea's salt is made of two parts: sodium and chloride. Joined together, they make sodium chloride, the same thing as the [[@salt|salt]] on your table. Seawater also holds magnesium, sulphate, calcium and potassium, plus tiny traces of almost everything, even gold. The gold is spread so thinly that nobody has found a way to collect it for a profit.

sec.h: Why the sea doesn't keep getting saltier
sec.t:
If rivers keep adding salt, you might expect the sea to grow saltier every year. Scientists think its saltiness has stayed fairly steady for a very long time. That is because salt also leaves the sea. Some settles into mud on the sea floor and slowly turns into rock. Some is taken up by sea creatures that build shells. Over long stretches of time, what comes in and what goes out roughly balance.

Saltiness does change from place to place. The Red Sea is extra salty, because the hot Sun evaporates a lot of water and few rivers flow in. The Baltic Sea, fed by many rivers and melting snow, is much less salty. These differences matter. Cold, salty water is heavy and sinks, which helps drive slow currents through the deep sea, as you can read in [[@ocean-currents|ocean currents]]. From 2011 to 2015, a NASA satellite called Aquarius mapped the saltiness of the sea's surface from space, month by month.

Some lakes are far saltier than any ocean. [[@dead-sea|The Dead Sea]], between Jordan and Israel, is almost ten times saltier than seawater. People float in it easily, like corks, because salty water is denser and pushes up harder. Utah's Great Salt Lake in the USA is also much saltier than the ocean. Water flows into these lakes but has no way out except by evaporating, so the salt keeps piling up.

sec.h: Salt from the sea in India
sec.t:
India makes most of its salt by drying seawater or salty groundwater. In the Little [[@gujarat-rann|Rann of Kutch]], salt workers called Agariyas pump salty water into shallow pans and wait for the Sun to do its work. After weeks of raking, the pans turn white with crystals. It is hard work in fierce heat. Together, Gujarat's [[@salt-pans|salt pans]] produce roughly three-quarters of all India's salt.

Salt has also shaped India's history. In 1930, Mahatma [[@gandhi|Gandhi]] walked about 390 km to the coastal village of Dandi to make salt from seawater, breaking a British law that [[@taxes|taxed]] it. That protest, the [[@salt-march|Salt March]], drew attention around the world to India's freedom struggle.

text: Block printing is a way of stamping patterns onto cloth or paper using carved blocks. A craftsman carves a design into a flat block of wood so that the pattern stands up from the surface. The printer presses the block into dye or paint, then onto the cloth, again and again, to make a repeating [[motif|motif]].

Each colour usually needs its own block. To print a red and black flower, the printer first stamps the black outline all along the cloth. Then they take a second block and fill in the red, lining it up exactly. It sounds simple, but doing it neatly across many metres takes years of practice.

st.prompt: A printer wants a flower with red petals, green leaves and a black outline. How many carved blocks will they need?

options.t: Three, one for each colour
One, painted in three colours
Six, two for every colour

st.reveal: Each colour usually needs its own block. The outline block often goes first, then the others fill in the colours. The printer must line each one up exactly over the last print, or the colours spill outside the lines.

d.try: Cut a potato in half with an adult's help. Ask the adult to carve a simple shape, like a star or leaf, so it stands out on the cut face. Dab it in poster paint and stamp a repeating pattern across an old T-shirt or a sheet of paper. Try to keep the spacing even.
myth: Hand block printing has been completely replaced by machines.

Machine and screen printing are faster and more common, but thousands of families in India still print cloth by hand. Many buyers pay more for the slight differences that show each piece was made by a person.
facts: usually carved from hardwood such as teak or sheesham

sec.t:
Blocks are usually carved from hardwoods like teak or sheesham, which do not crack or swell easily when wet. The carver draws the design on the smooth face, then chips away everything else with tiny chisels, leaving the lines raised.

A detailed block can take days to carve. Small holes are often drilled through it so trapped air can escape, giving a cleaner print. A good block can be used for years. Some printing families keep old blocks for generations, like a library of patterns.

Near [[@jaipur|Jaipur]], the villages of Sanganer and Bagru have printed cloth for centuries. Sanganer is known for delicate flowers on white backgrounds. Bagru printers often use *dabu*, a sticky mud paste stamped on to block the dye. Where the mud sits, the cloth stays pale, making soft, cracked patterns.

In [[@india-wonder-kutch-crafts|Kutch]], Gujarat, and across the border in Sindh, printers make *ajrakh*. It is printed on both sides in deep red and indigo blue, with star-like geometric patterns. Making ajrakh involves many stages of printing, dyeing, washing and drying, often over a couple of weeks. Running water is needed for the washing, and families have sometimes moved villages to find it.

Indian printed [[@clothes-cotton|cotton]] was traded across the Indian Ocean for centuries. At Fustat, an old part of Cairo, [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] found many scraps of Indian block-printed cloth, some made centuries ago in Gujarat. They show that ordinary people in Egypt wore Indian prints, as you can read in [[@textiles-india|How did Indian cloth amaze the world?]].

People in China used carved wooden blocks to print on paper long before Europe had printing. The oldest dated printed book in the world, the *Diamond Sutra*, was printed in China in 868 CE using woodblocks. It is now in the British Library in London.

In Japan, artists made colourful woodblock prints of landscapes and actors. The most famous, Katsushika Hokusai's *The Great Wave*, shows a [[@waves-how|huge wave]] curling over boats with [[@mount-fuji|Mount Fuji]] behind. It was printed in thousands of copies around 1831. Later, metal type and the [[@printing-press|printing press]] made printing words much faster, but carved blocks never disappeared.

text: A picture is flat, but your brain is easy to fool. Artists use the same clues your eyes rely on in real life. Faraway things look smaller. Closer things hide things behind them. Distant hills look paler and bluer.

The most powerful trick is called linear perspective. Parallel lines, like the two rails of a railway track, seem to meet at a single spot on the horizon, called the vanishing point. Draw your lines heading to that point, and a flat page suddenly seems to open up like a window.
Around 1415 in Florence, Italy, the architect Filippo Brunelleschi showed how to do this with mathematical precision.

spots: Lines going away from you all seem to meet at one point. Artists use this to draw roads, rails and rooms.
The same-sized trees are drawn smaller as they get farther away.
Faraway hills look paler and bluer, because there's more air between you and them. That's the same reason the sky is blue!
Things in front hide things behind. Your brain uses this to judge depth.

quiz.prompt: In a landscape, why do the farthest hills look pale and bluish?

quiz.reveal: Air scatters blue light more than red. The farther away a hill is, the more of that blue haze sits between you and it. Painters copy the effect to make distance look real.

d.try: Stand at a window with a view of a road, a row of buildings or a corridor. Close one eye and keep your head still. With a washable marker, trace the main lines you see straight onto the glass. Then look at your tracing. The lines going away from you should tilt towards one spot, the vanishing point. Wipe the glass clean afterwards.
myth: Before the Renaissance, artists drew "wrong" because they didn't understand depth.
Many artists chose other ways of showing space on purpose. Roman wall painters could suggest depth, and Mughal, Chinese and Egyptian artists followed their own rules to show what mattered most.

often several viewpoints in one picture

sec.t:
Brunelleschi painted a small picture of a building in Florence, the Baptistery, using his new rules. Then he drilled a hole through the painting. A viewer stood in front of the real Baptistery, looked through the hole from the back, and held up a mirror. In the mirror they saw the painting, lined up with the real building behind it. The painting is now lost, but his biographer wrote that it was hard to tell picture from reality.

In 1435, Leon Battista Alberti wrote the rules down in a book called *On Painting*. Within a generation, artists across Italy were using vanishing points, and the [[@renaissance|Renaissance]] had one of its favourite tools.

Look at a range of hills on a clear day and the farthest ones look paler and bluer than the nearest. That's because there is more air between you and them. Air scatters blue light more than red, the same reason the [[@sky-blue|sky is blue]]. The farther away something is, the more of that blue haze sits in front of it.

Painters call this aerial or atmospheric perspective. [[@leonardo|Leonardo da Vinci]] wrote about it in his notebooks and used it in the misty, blue-green landscape behind the *[[@mona-lisa|Mona Lisa]]*. You can see the same effect from a hill station in the [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]], where ridge after ridge fades into blue.

Linear perspective is one way to show space, not the only one. [[@mughal-miniatures|Mughal miniature]] painters often showed several viewpoints in a single picture. A palace courtyard might be seen from above, while the people in it are shown from the side, and a garden pool tilts up so you can see the fish. This let a painter show far more of a scene than one fixed eye could.

Many Chinese scroll painters also avoided a single vanishing point, so a viewer could wander through a landscape as the scroll unrolled. In the 20th century, [[@picasso|Pablo Picasso]] broke the rules on purpose, painting a face from the front and the side at once. Each of these is a choice about what a picture should do.

text: Judges decide disputes. When two people, two companies, or a person and the government disagree about what the law says or what really happened, they can go to court. A judge listens to both sides, looks at the evidence, and decides according to the law.

The key rule is fairness. A judge must not take sides in advance or decide because of who someone is. In criminal cases, the accused person is treated as innocent until the evidence proves otherwise. A judge's decision is called a [[verdict|verdict]] or a judgement.

sec.t:
Most cases start in a local court. In India, these are district courts. If someone thinks the decision was wrong, they can appeal to a higher court, which checks the reasoning. Above the district courts are 25 High Courts, and at the very top is the [[@supreme-courts|Supreme Court]] in Delhi.

The United States has two ladders side by side, one for each state's laws and one for [[federal|federal]] laws. Both lead up to the US Supreme Court in Washington, D.C., where nine justices sit together.

The highest courts have a special job. They check whether laws and government actions follow the [[@constitution|Constitution]]. If [[@parliament-india|Parliament]] passes a law that breaks someone's fundamental rights, a court can strike it down. This is called judicial review.

That is why judges need to be independent. In the US, federal judges serve for life unless removed for serious wrongdoing, so they need not fear losing their jobs for an unpopular decision. Indian Supreme Court judges retire at 65, and they too can be removed only through a hard process in Parliament.

In the US, many trials use a [[@jury|jury]], often 12 ordinary citizens chosen at random, who decide whether the accused is guilty. The judge runs the trial and decides the punishment. India once used juries too, but after a famous Bombay case in 1959, in which a jury's verdict was overturned by the High Court, the country phased them out. Now Indian judges decide on their own.

sec.h: Robes, symbols and a long queue
sec.t:
Indian judges and lawyers wear black robes with white neckbands, a habit inherited from British courts. A statue of Lady Justice, a woman holding scales, stands in many courts worldwide. Traditionally she is blindfolded, to show the law does not care who you are. In 2024, a new statue in India's Supreme Court library showed her with open eyes, holding the Constitution instead of a sword.

India's courts are very busy. More than 4 crore cases are waiting to be decided, and some take years. People often say "justice delayed is justice denied", and reducing these delays is one of the biggest jobs facing India's judges and [[@laws-made|lawmakers]].

text: People speak about 7,000 languages today. Ethnologue, a catalogue run by linguists (people who study languages), lists a little over 7,000 living ones.

That number hides a big imbalance. About two dozen languages, such as [[@chinese-characters|Mandarin Chinese]], Spanish, English and [[@hindi-language|Hindi]], are spoken by more than half the people on Earth. Thousands of others are spoken by a single village or a few hundred people.
The count is never exact. Linguists argue over where one language stops and a [[dialect|dialect]] begins, and a few languages in remote forests have barely been recorded.

d.try: Make a "hello" chart. Ask everyone in your family, building or class how to say hello in every language they know, and write each one down with the language's name. Count how many you collect. In many Indian classrooms the total passes ten.
myth: Some languages are simple or primitive, with hardly any grammar.

Linguists have never found a primitive language. Every language studied, whether written or only spoken, has full grammar and can say anything its speakers need. Some languages without writing have grammar far more complicated than English.

sec.t:
Hindi and [[@arabic-script|Urdu]] sound almost the same in daily speech, yet they use different scripts and are counted as two languages. Chinese "dialects" such as Mandarin and Cantonese can be harder for each other's speakers to follow than Hindi and Urdu.

So the line between a language and a dialect is partly about history, politics and pride. A famous joke among linguists, made popular by the scholar Max Weinreich, says a language is a dialect with an army and a navy.

Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers, people who learned it as their first language at home. Spanish comes second. English has fewer native speakers than either, but if you add everyone who learned it at school or at work, it has the most speakers in total, well over a billion.

Hindi is among the top few too, especially when you count the many people in India who speak it as a second or third language. [[@bengali-language|Bengali]], spoken in West Bengal and Bangladesh, also has more native speakers than Russian or Japanese.

A language often spreads because of trade, [[empire|empire]], films or the internet, not because it is easier to learn. English spread with British ships and later with American films, songs and computers.

Roughly 4 in 10 of the world's languages are [[endangered|endangered]], meaning children are no longer learning them. When grandparents are the last fluent speakers, a language can vanish within a lifetime. With it go songs, jokes, names for plants and ways of seeing the world.

India has its own fading voices. Great Andamanese, spoken in the [[@andaman|Andaman Islands]], now has only a handful of speakers left. In North America, many Native American languages are in the same position, though tribes are running schools and apps to bring them back.

Not every language is spoken aloud. Deaf communities around the world use well over a hundred [[@sign-language|sign languages]], each with its own grammar. American Sign Language and Indian Sign Language are separate languages, and a signer of one cannot simply understand the other.

Languages borrow from one another all the time. English took "shampoo", "pyjamas" and "jungle" from Indian languages, and Hindi took "school" and "station" from English. Some languages have even been used as secret codes, as the Navajo [[@code-talkers|code talkers]] showed in the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]]. A language that stops changing is usually one that nobody speaks any more.

text: Around the world, most children's days follow a familiar pattern: wake up, eat, go to school, play, help at home and sleep. But the details vary in surprising ways. Some children clean their own classrooms. Some learn over the internet from a sheep farm hundreds of kilometres from the nearest town. Some take a boat to school.

At the same time, not every child gets a school day at all. UNESCO estimated in 2025 that about 272 million children and teenagers were out of school, many because of poverty, conflict or because they have to work.

sec.h: Brooms in Japan, school at seven in Finland
sec.t:
In Japan, there are usually no cleaners in primary schools. After lunch, pupils grab brooms and cloths and sweep floors, wipe desks and even clean toilets. It's called o-soji, and the idea is that everyone looks after shared spaces. Many Japanese children also serve lunch to their classmates, wearing white coats and caps.

In Finland, children usually start formal school at seven, later than in most countries. School days for young children are short, homework is light and children spend long breaks playing outdoors, even in snow. Yet Finland has often scored highly in international tests.

sec.h: School from home in the Outback
sec.t:
Australia's Outback is so empty that some families live hundreds of kilometres from a school. Since 1951, the School of the Air in Alice Springs has taught them from a distance. Children once used two-way radios to talk to their teachers. Today they log in online. Students meet their classmates in person only a few times a year.

In Germany, children starting school on their first day get a Schultüte, a big paper cone filled with sweets, pencils and small presents. In France, many primary schools close on Wednesday afternoons, or all Wednesday, for sports and clubs.

In many countries, children help with chores before or after school, like fetching water, feeding animals, minding younger siblings or helping in a family shop. In rural areas of many countries, including parts of India, some children walk several kilometres each way to school. Bicycle schemes, like those that gave free cycles to schoolgirls in Bihar from 2006, helped many more girls stay in class.

Children everywhere also play. Tag, marbles, skipping and hide-and-seek turn up on every continent with different names and rules. And while one child is sitting down to breakfast, another, on the other side of the world, is going to bed. The Earth's [[@time-zones|time zones]] mean that somewhere, at every moment, a school day is just beginning. Kids' rights to school and play are part of the [[@rights-kids|rights of every child]], agreed by almost every country in 1989.

text: Money comes in a huge range of shapes, sizes and materials. Some coins have holes in the middle. Some notes are made of plastic you can see through. Swiss banknotes are designed to be read standing up, like a phone screen. All US dollar notes, from $1 to $100, are exactly the same size, while Indian notes get bigger as their value goes up.

Every country decorates its money with things it is proud of: leaders, animals, buildings, inventions and art. Look closely at any note and you'll find tiny details meant to stop forgers, and to help people who can't see well.

Most notes are made of cotton, sometimes mixed with linen, which is far tougher than wood-pulp paper. Many countries now use thin plastic film instead.

sec.t:
Turn over an Indian banknote and you'll find a panel with its value written in 15 languages, from Assamese to Urdu. Add Hindi and English on the front, and that makes 17. Indian notes also show a famous place on the back: the Red Fort, Hampi's stone chariot, the Rani ki Vav stepwell, and, on the ₹2,000 note withdrawn in 2023, the [[@isro-missions|Mangalyaan]] spacecraft.

The rupee got its own symbol, ₹, in 2010. It was designed by D. Udaya Kumar, who mixed the Devanagari letter "र" with the Roman "R".

On Yap, an island in the western Pacific, people used giant stone discs called rai. Some are more than 3 metres across, taller than a grown-up, with a hole in the middle for a pole. They were carved from rock on islands hundreds of kilometres away and brought back by canoe.

Big rai stones were so heavy that they stayed where they were. When one changed owners, everyone simply remembered who owned it. That's a little like a bank today, keeping a record instead of moving cash.

In 2009, Zimbabwe printed a note for 100 trillion dollars. That's 100 followed by 12 zeros. Prices had been rising so fast that the money was almost worthless. Reports at the time said one note was not enough for a bus ride in the capital, Harare. This kind of runaway [[@inflation|inflation]] shows that a note is only worth what people trust it to buy.

Indian coins and notes are designed to help people with low vision. Each note has a different size and raised marks you can feel, and the RBI launched a free phone app called MANI in 2020 that reads a note's value aloud. Coins of different values have different shapes, sizes and edges.

Canada puts raised dots on its notes. US notes, which are all the same size, have been criticised for being hard to tell apart, and the government has promised to add features to help.

In many places, people now pay with phones and cards more than cash. India's [[@upi-payments|UPI payments]] handle billions of transactions every month, from shopping malls to street vendors with a QR code taped to their cart. Sweden is one of the most cashless countries anywhere.

Still, notes and coins aren't disappearing yet. They work when phones die and networks fail. They're also tiny works of art. Each new note is designed over years, with hidden threads, colour-changing ink and watermarks, and making one that is hard to copy is a science of its own.

text: Children lose 20 baby teeth, usually between about ages 6 and 12. Almost every culture has a custom for what to do with them. In the US, UK and Canada, a tooth fairy swaps a tooth under the pillow for a coin or note. In Spain and Latin America, a mouse called Ratoncito Pérez does it. In India, Greece and many other countries, children throw their teeth onto the roof and ask a bird for a strong new one.
These customs share one wish: that the new tooth will grow in strong and straight. Many link teeth to animals with famously tough teeth, such as mice and rats.

sec.t:
Mice and rats have front teeth that never stop growing. That may be why so many tooth customs feature them. In France and Belgium, La Petite Souris, the little mouse, takes teeth and leaves a gift.

In Spain, the mouse has a name and a home. In 1894, the writer Luis Coloma wrote a story for the young King Alfonso XIII, who was eight and had just lost a tooth. In the story, Ratoncito Pérez lived in a biscuit tin in Madrid. Today a small plaque marks the spot on Calle del Arenal, and there's a little museum about the mouse nearby.

sec.h: Where the tooth fairy came from
sec.t:
The tooth fairy is fairly new. The idea grew in the US in the early 1900s. A short play called *The Tooth Fairy* appeared in 1927, and the custom spread through books, cartoons and ads in the decades after.

It may have mixed older European customs of burying teeth or giving them to mice with stories of [[@fairy-tales|fairies]]. Today the tooth fairy is popular across the US, the UK, Canada and Australia, and children in Indian cities increasingly know her too.

Each year a dental insurance company, Delta Dental, asks American parents how much the tooth fairy leaves. In its 2026 poll, the average was $5.84 per tooth, up from $5.01 the year before. The first tooth often earns more.

Back in 1998, the average was only about $1.30. Like everything else, the tooth fairy's prices go up with [[@inflation|inflation]]. Some economists even joke that her payments track the stock market.

sec.h: Why we lose teeth at all
sec.t:
A baby's jaw is small, so baby teeth are small too. As the face grows, there's room for bigger, stronger adult teeth. They grow underneath and press against the roots of baby teeth, which slowly [[dissolve|dissolve]]. That's why a lost baby tooth has hardly any root.

Humans get just two sets of [[@teeth|teeth]]. Sharks keep growing new ones all their lives, losing thousands. Elephants get six sets of molars and can starve if the last set wears out.

Mice and rats, meanwhile, have it the other way round. Their front teeth keep growing forever, and they must gnaw constantly to stop them getting too long, which is why so many children's stories trust them with lost teeth.

text: Writing was invented separately in several places, including [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], Egypt, [[@china-today|China]] and Central America. The oldest known comes from [[@sumer|Sumer]], in today's Iraq, about 5,200 years ago.

It began as a way to keep accounts. Temple officials needed to track how much grain, beer and how many sheep came in and went out. Over centuries, the marks grew into full writing that could record laws, letters, prayers and stories.

The [[@indus-script|Indus script]] is one of history's great unsolved puzzles. Thousands of seals exist, but nobody can read them. Brahmi script, used by Emperor [[@ashoka|Ashoka]], grew into Devanagari, Tamil, [[@bengali-language|Bengali]] and many other scripts used today.

sec.t:
Before writing, people in Mesopotamia used small clay tokens to count goods: a cone for a measure of grain, perhaps a disc for a sheep. Some tokens were sealed inside clay envelopes, with their shapes pressed on the outside so people could check without breaking them.

The [[archaeologist|archaeologist]] Denise Schmandt-Besserat argued that this led to writing. Why make tokens at all, if marks on clay could do the job? Soon scribes were pressing signs into flat tablets with a cut reed. This wedge-shaped writing is called cuneiform.

In Egypt, picture-writing called [[@hieroglyphs|hieroglyphs]] appeared at about the same time as cuneiform. Nobody could read it for over 1,400 years, until the Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, carried the same message in [[hieroglyphs|hieroglyphs]] and Greek. Jean-François Champollion cracked it in 1822.

In China, the oldest known writing appears on "oracle bones" from over 3,000 years ago, used to ask questions of ancestors. Modern [[@chinese-characters|Chinese characters]] descend from them. In Central America, [[@myths-maya|the Maya]] developed a full writing system that scholars mostly decoded only in the late 1900s.

About 3,000 years ago, traders called [[@phoenicians|the Phoenicians]], living on the coast of today's Lebanon, used a short set of letters, each standing for one sound. It had only about 22 signs, far fewer than cuneiform's hundreds.

The Greeks borrowed it and added vowels. Latin came from Greek, and the letters you are reading now come from Latin. Some secret writing systems later scrambled these letters into [[@cipher-codes|codes]].

The Indus seals, about 4,600 years old, carry short rows of signs, usually only about five long. Some scholars think they are full writing, others think they are symbols, like logos. Without a longer text or a stone carrying the same words in a known language, nobody can be sure. Computer scientists and linguists keep trying, and new seals still turn up in excavations.

Brahmi appears on Ashoka's rock and pillar messages from about 2,300 years ago. It too was forgotten, until a British scholar, James Prinsep, worked it out in 1837. From Brahmi grew most of the [[@scripts-india|scripts of India]] and many in Southeast Asia, from Thai to Tibetan.

text: Bollywood dance grew out of Hindi films, where songs and dances have been part of the story since sound arrived in Indian cinema in 1931. Choreographers mixed steps from [[@indian-classical-dance|classical dance]], village folk dances and Western styles like disco and hip-hop. The result was bright, energetic and easy to enjoy even if you didn't understand the words.

It spread through the millions of Indians living abroad, who carried films and music with them. Weddings, college clubs and fitness classes picked it up. By the 2000s you could take a Bollywood dance class in New York, London or Sydney, often taught by people who had never been to India.

sec.t:
When Alam Ara came out in 1931 as India's first sound film, it had several songs. Audiences loved them, and songs soon became a normal part of Hindi films. Actors usually mimed to recordings by playback singers, so the stars were free to dance.

A film song is often a little break from the plot. A couple falls in love, and suddenly they are dancing in a Swiss meadow. A festival scene turns into a crowd of a hundred dancers. These numbers were filmed with care, and many people remember the songs long after they forget the story.

Behind every famous dance is a choreographer, the person who designs the steps. Saroj Khan created many classic numbers, including "Ek Do Teen" in Tezaab (1988), and was known for expressive faces as much as footwork.

Farah Khan choreographed "Chaiyya Chaiyya" for Dil Se (1998). The dancers performed on the roof of a train on the [[@india-wonder-toy-train|Nilgiri Mountain Railway]] in Tamil Nadu, held by hidden safety ropes. Later she worked on stage shows abroad too, helping carry the style to new audiences.

[[@indian-diaspora|Indian families abroad]] kept watching Hindi films on video and satellite TV, and danced to the songs at weddings and festivals. Their children formed dance teams at American and British universities, where Bollywood fusion competitions became popular.

In 2009, the song "Jai Ho" from the British film Slumdog Millionaire, with music by A. R. Rahman, won an Oscar. Its dance finale in a Mumbai railway station was seen around the world. In 2023, "Naatu Naatu" from the Telugu film RRR won the Oscar for Best Original Song. RRR isn't a Bollywood film, but its dance showed how much the world now loved Indian film dance in general.

Hindi films aren't the only Indian films with famous dances. Telugu, Tamil and other [[@cinema-south|South Indian cinemas]] have their own dance stars and styles. Prabhu Deva, from Tamil films, became famous for his rubbery, lightning-quick moves.

Today these styles borrow from each other all the time. A dance step from a Telugu hit might turn up in a Hindi film a year later, and then in a dance class in Chicago.

text: Esports are video games played as competitive sports. Professional players and teams compete in organised leagues and [[tournament|tournaments]], often for big prizes. Matches are streamed online and shown in arenas, with commentators, replays and cheering fans, much like a cricket or football match.

Popular esports games include League of Legends, Valorant, Counter-Strike, Dota 2 and Fortnite. In India, mobile games such as Battlegrounds Mobile India (BGMI) are hugely popular. Many are played by teams of four or five, though some, like fighting games, are one against one. Esports have become big enough to appear at the Asian Games.

sec.t:
In October 1972, students at Stanford University in California held an "Intergalactic Spacewar Olympics". They played *Spacewar!*, one of the earliest [[@video-game-history|computer games]], and the prize was a year's subscription to *Rolling Stone* magazine.

In 1980 the company Atari held a Space Invaders championship in the USA, and thousands of players took part. In the late 1990s and 2000s, faster internet let players compete online. [[@seoul|South Korea]] built TV channels and arenas for games like StarCraft, and players there became celebrities.

People argue about whether esports are "real" sports. They do not need much physical strength. But they need very fast [[@reflexes|reflexes]], quick decisions, teamwork and hours of practice. Top players can make hundreds of precise mouse clicks and key presses a minute.

Many teams train like athletes. They have coaches who study opponents, analysts who review recordings and fitness trainers. Players are encouraged to exercise, sleep well and take breaks, because tired players make mistakes. Careers are often short. Many professionals retire in their mid-twenties, when their [[@sport-science-reaction-time|reaction times]] begin to slow slightly, and move into coaching, commentating or streaming.

India's esports scene has grown fast, especially through smartphones and cheap mobile data. Many fans first played on their phones. In 2018, esports were a demonstration event at the Asian Games in Jakarta. At the Hangzhou Asian Games, held in 2023, they were a full medal event.

In December 2022 the Government of India said esports would be treated as part of multi-sport events, under the sports ministry. In 2025 India passed a law that bans online games played for real money, while supporting esports and other skill-based games.

Doctors and parents worry about too much [[@screen-time|screen time]]. Sitting for hours can strain eyes, wrists and backs, and late-night gaming can harm sleep. Most experts suggest regular breaks, good posture and a balance with outdoor play.

The International Olympic Committee has also shown interest in esports, and has talked about holding Olympic Esports Games, though plans have changed more than once. For now, most young players will enjoy games as a hobby. The few who turn pro usually say it takes far more discipline than people expect.

text: Humans [[evolve|evolved]] in Africa. Over millions of years, a branch of the ape family slowly changed into the many kinds of early humans that scientists call hominins. Only one of those kinds survives today: us, Homo sapiens.

The oldest [[fossil|fossils]] of our own [[species|species]], found at Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, are about 300,000 years old. From Africa, groups of modern humans spread across the world, reaching Asia, including [[@early-humans-india|India]], Australia, Europe and finally the Americas. This idea, built from fossils, stone tools and DNA, is often called the "Out of Africa" story.

sec.t:
Our family split from the line leading to chimpanzees roughly 6–7 million years ago. One of the first big changes was walking upright on two legs.

At Laetoli in Tanzania, the team of the British scientist Mary Leakey found a trail of footprints in 1978. They were made about 3.6 million years ago by upright walkers crossing damp volcanic ash, which then hardened. The prints look surprisingly like ours.

In 1974, in Ethiopia, scientists found much of the skeleton of a small female about 3.2 million years old. They nicknamed her Lucy, after a Beatles song playing in their camp. Lucy walked upright but had a small brain, about the size of a chimpanzee's.

When modern humans spread out of Africa, they met Neanderthals and Denisovans. [[dna|DNA]] shows that they sometimes had children together. The Swedish scientist Svante Pääbo won the 2022 Nobel Prize for reading the DNA of Neanderthals from ancient bones.

Today most people with ancestry outside Africa carry a little Neanderthal DNA, and some groups in Asia and Oceania carry Denisovan DNA too. The Neanderthals themselves died out about 40,000 years ago.

The evidence comes from several directions. Fossils show how bodies changed. Layers of volcanic ash around them can be dated using the slow, steady decay of [[radioactive|radioactive]] [[element|elements]]. Stone tools and hearths show what people did. DNA from living people works like a family tree: groups that split apart long ago have built up more differences. When all these clues point the same way, scientists grow more confident. When they clash, a new debate begins.

Modern humans had reached South Asia at least 50,000–70,000 years ago. Stone tools found at Jwalapuram in Andhra Pradesh may be even older, though scientists argue about who made them. Today, India has some of the greatest genetic variety outside Africa, a sign of a long and rich human history.

People reached the Americas much later, probably crossing from Siberia into Alaska. Footprints at White Sands in New Mexico may be over 20,000 years old, though some scientists question those dates.

Along the way, humans created [[@cave-art|cave paintings]], music and stories. [[@genes-family|Genes]] carry traces of this whole journey in every person alive today.

text: When you cut yourself, your body runs a repair job in four overlapping stages.

First it stops the bleeding. Blood vessels narrow, and tiny cell pieces called [[platelet|platelets]] stick together over the gap, held by a mesh of [[protein|protein]] threads. This forms a clot. When the clot dries on the surface, it becomes a scab.

Next, white blood cells clean out germs and dirt, which is why a cut can look red and puffy. Then new skin cells and fresh tissue grow in to fill the gap. Finally, over months, the repair is strengthened and tidied. A small cut is closed within days. A deeper one may [[@power-axolotl|leave a scar]].

st.reveal: A covered wound stays slightly moist, which makes it easier for new skin cells to slide across the gap. Left to dry out, the wound forms a hard scab that new cells have to burrow under, which takes longer.

d.try: With an adult's permission, look at an old scar on someone's knee or elbow with a magnifying glass. Compare it with the skin next to it. You may see that the scar is smoother and shinier, with no fine hairs and fewer lines, because scar tissue is built differently from ordinary skin.
myth: You should let a cut "breathe" in the open air so it dries out and heals faster.
Small wounds usually heal faster, and leave smaller scars, when they are kept clean and covered so they stay slightly moist. Ask a trusted adult to help clean and cover a cut.

sec.t:
Over the next few days, your [[@immune-system|immune system]] gets to work. Extra blood flows to the area, bringing white blood cells that swallow [[bacteria|bacteria]] and dead cells. The area may feel warm, look pink and be a little sore.

This is normal. But sometimes a cut gets more painful, swells a lot, oozes pus or has red streaks spreading from it. Then it may be infected, and a trusted adult should get a doctor to look at it. People with a condition called haemophilia have blood that doesn't clot properly, so even small cuts need extra care.

Under the scab, cells at the edges of the wound start to multiply and crawl across the gap. Other cells lay down [[collagen|collagen]], a tough protein that acts like scaffolding. Tiny new blood vessels grow into the area to feed it.

When the gap is covered with new [[@skin|skin]], the scab has nothing left to do and falls off on its own. Picking it off early tears away new cells and can make a scar more likely.

For a long time, many people believed cuts should be left open to dry. In 1962, a British scientist, George Winter, tested this on young pigs, whose skin is a lot like ours. Wounds that were covered healed about twice as fast as wounds left open to the air.

This led to the modern plasters and dressings that keep a wound clean and slightly moist. Good [[@first-aid|first aid]] for a small cut is simple: wash it with [[@water-purify|clean water]], press to stop bleeding, and cover it.

A deep cut may need stitches, [[@glue-sticky|glue]] or strips that hold the edges together, so there is less gap to fill. [[surgeon|Surgeons]] have been closing wounds this way for thousands of years. The ancient Indian surgeon [[@sushruta|Sushruta]] described stitching with thread.

Scar tissue is made of collagen laid down in a hurry, so it is less stretchy than normal skin. It has no hair or sweat [[gland|glands]]. Scars often fade over a year or two, but rarely vanish completely. Some people's scars grow large and raised, which doctors can help with.

text: A vaccine trains your [[@immune-system|immune system]] to recognise a germ. Where it is given decides where that training happens.

Germs like polio enter through the mouth and grow in the gut. A vaccine swallowed as drops builds defences, such as [[antibody|antibodies]], right there in the gut lining. Germs that travel in the blood, or enter through cuts or the lungs, are often better handled by an injection.

quiz.prompt: Polio germs enter through the mouth and multiply in the gut. Why might drops work especially well against them?

options.t: The drops train the gut itself to block the germ where it enters
Drops are stronger than injections for every disease
Swallowed medicine never reaches the blood

quiz.reveal: Oral polio vaccine sets up defences in the lining of the gut, exactly where the real virus would try to grow. That stops the virus from multiplying and spreading to other people. An injected vaccine protects the person well, but does less to block the virus in the gut.

myth: Injections always work better than drops.

It depends on the germ. For germs that enter through the gut, like polio, rotavirus and cholera, drops can build protection exactly where it is needed. Many countries use both kinds of polio vaccine together.

sec.t:
Drops are quick, painless and easy to give to crores of children in a few days. But the weakened virus in them can, very rarely, change and cause illness, especially where too few children are vaccinated. Injected vaccines with killed virus cannot do this.

So many countries now use both. India added injected polio vaccine to its routine schedule in 2015, alongside the drops. Using both gives strong protection in the blood and in the gut.

Polio is not the only one. Rotavirus, which causes severe tummy upsets in babies, is fought with drops too. Cholera, a germ spread by dirty water, has an oral vaccine. Some flu vaccines are sprayed into the nose, because that is where flu gets in.

Every vaccine is a clever shortcut for your body's defences. The world has already wiped out [[@smallpox|smallpox]], one of the deadliest [[@disease-history|diseases in history]], using vaccines. Polio may be next: wild polio now survives in only a very few places on Earth.

text: Non-stick coating was discovered by accident. On 6 April 1938, Roy Plunkett, a 27-year-old chemist at the DuPont company in New Jersey, USA, was working on new gases for refrigerators. He opened the valve on a cylinder of one gas, and nothing came out.

The cylinder still weighed as much as a full one. So he and his assistant cut it open. Inside was a waxy white powder. The gas had joined itself into a brand new solid that almost nothing would stick to. It was later named Teflon.

st.prompt: Roy Plunkett's gas cylinder seemed empty, but it still weighed as much as a full one. What had happened?

options.t: The gas had joined into a solid powder
The gas had leaked out and been replaced by air
The scale was broken

st.reveal: The small gas molecules had linked up into long chains, forming a solid. That solid was PTFE, now known as Teflon. Nothing came out of the valve because there was no gas left to flow.

d.try: With an adult, place a small drop of honey on a steel plate and another on a non-stick pan, both cold. Tilt each one slowly and watch which drop slides first. The non-stick surface gives the honey almost nothing to hold on to.
myth: Teflon was invented by NASA for the space programme.
Teflon was discovered by accident in 1938, two decades before NASA existed. NASA did use it later, including in the fabric of Apollo spacesuits, which may be how the myth started.
facts: 6 April 1938, by Roy Plunkett at DuPont, New Jersey, USA

sec.t:
The gas Plunkett used was made of small [[molecule|molecules]] of carbon and fluorine. Under the pressure and cold inside the cylinder, the molecules linked together into very long chains, like beads clipped into a necklace. Chemists call this kind of material a [[polymer|polymer]].

The new chains were wrapped tightly in fluorine [[atom|atoms]]. Fluorine holds onto carbon extremely firmly and barely reacts with anything else. That makes PTFE resistant to almost every chemical, and so slippery that water, oil and food slide straight off.

At first, nobody knew what to do with it. It was expensive, hard to shape and wouldn't stick to anything, which made it difficult to coat onto other surfaces.

Its first big job was secret. During the Second World War, scientists building the first atomic bombs needed seals and linings that could survive a fiercely corrosive gas made from uranium. PTFE was one of the few materials that could.

DuPont registered the name Teflon in 1945. After the war it found uses in wires, pipes and machine parts.

{{story:power-gecko-feet}}

sec.h: From fishing line to frying pan
sec.t:
The leap to the kitchen came from France. In the early 1950s, an engineer named Marc Grégoire coated his fishing line with PTFE so it wouldn't tangle. According to the family story, his wife Colette suggested he try it on her cooking pans.

He worked out how to make it grip aluminium, and in 1956 he started the company Tefal. Its name joins "Teflon" and "aluminium". Non-stick pans arrived in American shops in the early 1960s and soon spread worldwide, including to India, where a non-stick tawa now makes dosas slide off with very little oil.

PTFE has one of the lowest [[@friction|friction]] levels of any solid. A block of it sliding on more PTFE feels almost as slick as wet ice on wet ice.

[[@power-gecko-feet|Geckos]] climb walls using millions of tiny hairs on their toes, which cling to surfaces using weak forces between molecules. On Teflon, those forces are too weak to hold them. Scientists studying geckos have even used Teflon to test the limits of their grip.

NASA used PTFE coatings in the outer fabric of Apollo [[@spacesuits|spacesuits]], which helped start the myth that Teflon came from space research. It also coats the giant fabric roofs of some stadiums, because rain and dirt slide right off.

Doctors use PTFE in some artificial blood vessels and stitches, since the body tends to leave it alone.

Non-stick pans are safe for everyday cooking. But if an empty pan is overheated, above about 260°C, the coating can start to break down and give off fumes. These can make people feel ill and can kill pet birds, whose lungs are very sensitive. So cooks are advised not to heat non-stick pans empty on high flame, and to throw away badly scratched ones.

There was another concern. A chemical called PFOA was once used to make Teflon, and it lingers in the environment. In the USA, major makers agreed to phase it out, and they stopped using it by 2015.

Plunkett's "failed" experiment changed kitchens around the world. Thirty years later, at another American company, a chemist made a [[@accident-post-it|glue that wasn't sticky enough]], and that mistake turned out just as useful.

text: India's Constitution was written by the Constituent Assembly, a body of Indian leaders that met from December 1946 to January 1950. Its Drafting Committee was led by Dr B.R. [[@ambedkar|Ambedkar]], a lawyer and social reformer often called the chief architect of the Constitution.

The members debated every article in public for almost three years. They studied [[constitution|constitutions]] from around the world, including those of the [[@us-constitution|United States]], Britain, Ireland and Canada, and argued over rights, languages, religion, the powers of states and much more. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950, the day India became a [[republic|republic]].

st.prompt: Why was 26 January chosen as the day India's Constitution came into force?

options.t: On that day in 1930, Congress had declared the goal of complete independence
It was the day the British left India
It was Ambedkar's birthday

st.reveal: On 26 January 1930, the Indian National Congress declared Purna Swaraj, complete independence, as its goal. Leaders chose the same date in 1950 to start the Constitution. Ambedkar's birthday is 14 April.

d.try: Write a short constitution for your class or family, with five rules everyone agrees on. Discuss each rule, change words until everyone is happy, then vote. Notice how long it takes for even five rules, and think about how the Assembly managed 395 articles.
myth: Dr Ambedkar wrote the whole Constitution alone.

Ambedkar led the Drafting Committee and guided the draft through the Assembly, which is why he is called the chief architect of the Constitution. But it was debated, changed and approved by nearly 300 members, with help from advisers such as B.N. Rau.

sec.t:
The Assembly first met on 9 December 1946 in the Constitution Hall in Delhi, now the Central Hall of Samvidhan Sadan. Most members were elected by the provincial assemblies, and others represented the [[@princely-states|princely states]]. After [[@partition|Partition]] in 1947, the number fell from 389 to 299.

Dr Rajendra Prasad, later India's first President, was chosen to chair it. Jawaharlal [[@nehru|Nehru]] moved the Objectives Resolution, setting out its goals. [[@sardar-patel|Sardar Patel]] led work on fundamental rights and on minorities. Fifteen members were women, including Hansa Mehta, Sucheta Kripalani, Ammu Swaminathan and Dakshayani Velayudhan, the only Dalit woman in the Assembly.

On 29 August 1947, the Assembly set up a Drafting Committee of seven members, with Ambedkar as chair. The constitutional adviser, B.N. Rau, had prepared an early draft, which the committee rewrote and expanded.

Ambedkar explained and defended each part of the draft in the Assembly, answering thousands of questions and proposed changes. Members put forward more than 7,000 [[amendment|amendments]], and about 2,500 were discussed. Ambedkar argued strongly that the Constitution must protect people from discrimination, including untouchability, which it abolished.

Instead of printing the final text, the Assembly had it handwritten. The [[@words-handwriting|calligrapher]] Prem Behari Narain Raizada wrote out the English version in flowing italic script, using hundreds of pen nibs. Artists from Santiniketan, led by [[@nandalal-bose|Nandalal Bose]], decorated the pages with paintings, from Indus seals to scenes of the Buddha and Mahatma Gandhi.

A Hindi version was hand-written separately by another calligrapher, Vasant Krishan Vaidya. Raizada asked for no fee, only that he be allowed to sign each page, and his name appears on every page of the English copy. On 24 January 1950, the members signed both copies. These originals are now kept in helium-filled cases in the [[@parliament-india|Parliament]] library.

When it began, the Constitution had 395 articles and 8 schedules. It is one of the longest written constitutions of any country. It has been [[@constitution-amendments|amended]] more than a hundred times since.

One Assembly member, Hansa Mehta, also served on the [[@united-nations|United Nations]] committee that wrote the Universal Declaration of [[@human-rights|Human Rights]]. She helped change its opening from "All men are born free and equal" to "All human beings are born free and equal". Every 26 November, India marks Constitution Day.

text: Huge wigs became fashion in Europe in the 1600s and 1700s for a mix of reasons. A French king went bald young and covered it up. A common disease of the time made many people's hair fall out. Lice were everywhere, and shaving your head and wearing a wig was easier than fighting them in your own hair. Then rich people copied the king, and wigs became a sign of power.
By the 1770s, some of the most fashionable women in Paris piled their hair and false hair into towers decorated with feathers, fruit, birds and even a model ship.

st.prompt: Why did many 1700s wig wearers dust their wigs with white powder?

options.t: White or grey hair was the fashionable look
The powder kept them cool in summer
It was a medicine against colds

st.reveal: Powdered white or grey wigs were the height of style, and the powder also helped hide smells. It was made from finely ground starch, often scented with lavender or orange flower.

src: Victoria and Albert Museum, London, collections on 18th-century dress.

n.certNote: Historians agree that a king going bald and a widespread disease that caused hair loss helped start the fashion. Reports of hairstyles a metre tall come partly from cartoons that may exaggerate.

Washington wore his own hair, grown long, tied back and dusted with white powder. Paintings make it look like a wig, but it wasn't.

sec.h: A bald king starts a trend
sec.t:
King Louis XIII of France began losing his hair in his twenties and started wearing a wig in the 1620s. His son, Louis XIV, had thick hair as a young man, but wore grand curly wigs for most of his long reign. When the king of the most powerful court in Europe wore something, the nobles copied it.

In England, King Charles II returned from exile in France in 1660 and brought the fashion with him. Soon any man who wanted to look important wore a wig. The best ones were made of human hair. Cheaper ones used horsehair or goat hair. That is where the word "bigwig" comes from, one of many [[@idioms|idioms]] that outlived the thing they described.

The most extreme styles appeared in Paris in the 1770s. Queen Marie Antoinette and her hairdresser helped make the *pouf* famous: hair stretched over a frame of wire and padding, then decorated. One style, made in 1778, carried a model of the French warship *La Belle Poule*.

How tall did they get? Cartoonists in London drew women whose hair touched the ceiling, but cartoons exaggerate. Real portraits suggest some reached around half a metre above the head. Women had to kneel in their carriages, and a style could stay in place for weeks.

After the [[@french-revolution|French Revolution]] began in 1789, looking like a rich aristocrat became risky. Short, natural hair came in.

Wigs are far older than Louis XIV. Thousands of years ago in [[@ancient-egypt|ancient Egypt]], many wealthy people shaved their heads to stay cool and avoid lice, then wore wigs of human hair and plant fibre for special occasions. Beeswax and resin held the curls in place. Some of these wigs survive in museums today, still with their braids.

Judges and lawyers in Britain kept their wigs long after everyone else gave them up. Many still wear horsehair wigs in criminal courts. Lawyers in India also once wore them under British rule, but dropped them long ago. The rest of us use our own hair, which grows about 1 cm a month. Why it keeps growing on your head but stops short on your arm comes down to tiny roots with different timers, explained in [[@hair-grow|how hair grows]].

text: Mexico is a large country between the United States and Central America. It is famous for its food, its ancient cities, its bright festivals and its art. But its biggest gift to the world may be the plants first farmed there.

[[@corn-maize|Maize]] (corn), [[@food-why-chillies-red|chillies]], tomatoes, beans, squash and avocados were all grown in or near Mexico thousands of years ago. Cocoa, the bean behind [[@chocolate-tree|chocolate]], was prized there too. Today these foods are eaten everywhere, from a bowl of [[@popcorn|popcorn]] in Chicago to a plate of [[@chillies|chilli]]-laced pav bhaji in Mumbai.

st.reveal: Chillies were grown in Mexico thousands of years ago. Portuguese traders brought them to India in the 1500s, and within a century they had spread through Indian cooking.

sec.t:
Corn did not exist in the wild. About 9,000 years ago, farmers in southern Mexico began choosing seeds from a scraggly grass called teosinte. Its "cob" held only a handful of hard seeds. Over thousands of years of picking the best plants, those farmers turned it into maize with fat, juicy cobs.

Maize became so important that Maya stories describe the first people being made from maize dough. Today it is one of the most grown crops on Earth, and makka roti with sarson ka saag owes its yellow colour to that grass from Mexico.

Every year on 1 and 2 November, many Mexican families celebrate the Day of the Dead (Día de los Muertos). They build altars at home with photos of relatives who have died, along with marigold flowers, [[@candles|candles]], sugar skulls and the person's favourite foods.

Paper banners with cut-out patterns hang over the streets, and bakeries sell a sweet bread decorated with strips of dough shaped like bones. Children get sugar skulls with their own names iced across the forehead.

It is a happy, colourful time, not a gloomy one. Families visit graves, tell stories and share meals. The marigolds are thought to guide the spirits home with their scent. UNESCO lists the festival as part of the world's intangible cultural heritage.

About 66 million years ago, an [[asteroid|asteroid]] around 10 km wide slammed into the sea off what is now Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. It left a [[crater|crater]], called Chicxulub, about 180 km across, now buried under rock and sea.

The impact threw so much dust and gas into the sky that it helped wipe out the large dinosaurs, as told in the story of [[@extinction|extinction]]. Not far away, the ruins of the Maya city of Chichén Itzá draw visitors who climb its stepped pyramid. Few realise they are standing near the scar of the most famous collision in Earth's history.

text: The Jain [[scripture|scriptures]] are called the Agamas. They record the teachings of [[@mahavira|Mahavira]], the 24th and last Tirthankara, or great spiritual teacher, of Jainism, who lived in eastern India about 2,500 years ago. His closest followers memorised his words, and monks passed them on by heart for centuries.

The two main Jain traditions see the Agamas differently. Svetambara Jains, whose monks and nuns wear white, believe a large part of the Agamas survives, in around 32 to 45 texts depending on the group. Digambara Jains believe the original Agamas were lost, and they treat other ancient works as their scriptures. Both honour a text called the Tattvartha Sutra, which sums up Jain teaching.

n.certNote: Jains agree the Agamas record the teachings of Mahavira, but the two main traditions disagree about which texts survive. Dates for Mahavira's life and for when the texts were written down are also debated by historians.

myth: Jainism is just a branch of Hinduism or Buddhism.

Jainism is a separate religion with its own teachers, beliefs and scriptures. It grew up in the same part of India at a similar time to Buddhism, and the three traditions share some ideas, but Jains have their own path.

sec.t:
Jainism is one of India's oldest religions. It teaches [[ahimsa|ahimsa]], not harming any living being, along with truthfulness, not stealing, self-control and not clinging to possessions. Jains believe every living thing, even a tiny insect, has a soul. The 2011 [[census|census]] counted about 45 lakh Jains in India. Large communities live in Gujarat, Maharashtra, Rajasthan and Karnataka, and others in the USA, the UK and East Africa.

According to tradition, Mahavira's chief disciples, called *ganadharas*, arranged his teachings into twelve groups called Angas, or limbs. Monks learned them by heart in Ardhamagadhi, an everyday language of the time, rather than in [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]].

Remembering huge texts word for word is hard. During [[famine|famines]], when monks scattered, parts were forgotten. Jain tradition says monks met several times to recite what they remembered and fix the texts.

{{story:mahavira}}

The Svetambara tradition says the most important meeting took place at Valabhi, in Gujarat, around 453 or 466 CE. Led by a teacher named Devarddhigani Kshamashramana, the monks wrote the surviving teachings down for the first time.

The collection includes eleven of the twelve Angas. The twelfth was already lost. The first Anga, the Acharanga Sutra, explains how monks and nuns should live, walk, eat and speak without harming living things. Other texts tell stories, discuss the soul and describe how the universe is arranged.

Digambara Jains don't accept these texts as the original Agamas. Instead they revere works such as the Shatkhandagama, composed in the early centuries CE, and the writings of the teacher Kundakunda, such as the Samayasara. Very old palm-leaf [[manuscript|manuscripts]] of the Shatkhandagama's commentaries are kept at Moodabidri in Karnataka.

One text bridges the two traditions. The Tattvartha Sutra, by a scholar called Umaswati, was written in Sanskrit, probably between the 2nd and 5th centuries CE. In short lines, it explains the soul, karma and the path to freedom from rebirth.

One of its lines, *Parasparopagraho jivanam*, means "souls render service to one another". It appears on the official Jain emblem and is often quoted as the heart of Jain [[ethics|ethics]]. The same care for all living things is why nearly all Jains are [[@vegetarian|vegetarian]], and many avoid root vegetables as well.

sec.h: Gold, blue and the Kalpa Sutra
sec.t:
The Kalpa Sutra tells the life of Mahavira and other Tirthankaras. Every year, during the festival of Paryushana, monks read it aloud to gatherings of Jains.

From about the 14th century, wealthy Jain families in Gujarat and Rajasthan paid for beautiful copies of it, painted with gold and deep blue. Giving a holy book to a temple was considered an act of great merit. Jain communities kept these manuscripts in special storerooms called *gyan bhandars*, "treasuries of knowledge". Some, like those in Jaisalmer and Patan, have protected palm-leaf and paper manuscripts for many centuries, making them among India's oldest working [[@libraries|libraries]].

text: Jules Verne was a French writer who lived from 1828 to 1905. He wrote adventure novels packed with science and travel, and he's often called one of the fathers of [[@science-fiction|science fiction]].

His characters go under the sea in a submarine, deep into the Earth through a volcano, around the world against the clock, and to the Moon in a giant shell. Verne studied science books, maps and engineering journals to make his adventures feel believable, even when they were impossible.
His books have been translated into dozens of languages. Long lists of the world's most translated authors put him near the very top.

sec.h: A boy from a harbour town
sec.t:
Verne grew up in Nantes, a busy port on the Loire river in western France. He watched sailing ships come and go and dreamed of faraway places. A family story says he once tried to sneak away as a ship's boy, but was caught and brought home.

His father was a lawyer and wanted his son to be one too. Verne studied law in Paris, but spent his time writing plays and reading about geography and science instead.

In 1863 a publisher, Pierre-Jules Hetzel, printed *Five Weeks in a Balloon*, about a journey across Africa by [[@hot-air-balloons|hot-air balloon]]. It was a hit. Hetzel signed Verne up to write novels for years to come.

Nemo means "nobody" in Latin. In *Twenty Thousand Leagues* he's a mystery, a brilliant man who hates [[empire|empires]]. Verne reveals the secret in a later book, *The Mysterious Island* (1875).

Nemo is Prince Dakkar, son of an Indian raja from Bundelkhand. After the [[@revolt-1857|revolt of 1857]], in which he fought the British, he escaped and built the *Nautilus* to live free beneath the sea.

In *Around the World in Eighty Days* (1872), the English gentleman Phileas Fogg bets he can circle the globe in 80 days. He crosses India by train and, when a railway line turns out to be unfinished, by elephant.

The book inspired real races. In 1889, the American journalist Nellie Bly set out to beat Fogg's time. She stopped in France to meet Verne on the way and finished in 72 days.

Verne didn't invent the submarine. Real ones existed before him. But his *From the Earth to the Moon* (1865) had three men launched from Florida. In 1968, the three astronauts of Apollo 8 launched from Florida too, and became the first humans to circle the Moon. Their capsule, like Verne's, splashed down in the Pacific.

One early novel, *Paris in the Twentieth Century*, imagined glass towers, petrol-driven cars and a worldwide [[telegraph|telegraph]] network. Hetzel turned it down, and it wasn't published until 1994. Still, Verne wasn't really trying to predict anything. He wanted readers to be thrilled by science and curious about the world. Many engineers, explorers and [[@apollo-moon|astronauts]] have said his books made them want to go and see for themselves.

text: Maya Angelou was an American writer, poet and civil rights worker. She is best known for *I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings* (1969), the story of her childhood. It was one of the first books by a Black American woman about her own life to become a bestseller.

She lived many lives. She was a dancer, a singer, a cook, a journalist in Africa, a teacher and a film director. In 1993 she read her poem "On the Pulse of Morning" at the inauguration of President Bill Clinton. In 2022 she became the first Black woman to appear on a US quarter-dollar coin.

st.prompt: Maya Angelou's most famous book takes its title from a poem by another Black American poet. What is it called?

options.t: I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings
Still I Rise
The Weary Blues

st.reveal: The title comes from the poem "Sympathy" by Paul Laurence Dunbar, written in 1899. In the poem a caged bird sings because it longs to be free. "Still I Rise" is one of Angelou's own poems, and The Weary Blues is by Langston Hughes.

sec.t:
She was born Marguerite Annie Johnson in 1928 in St. Louis, Missouri. "Maya" came from her brother Bailey, who called her "My" for "my sister". When their parents' marriage ended, the two small children were sent to live with their grandmother in Stamps, Arkansas, a small town where Black and white people lived separate lives by law.

When she was about eight, something frightening happened to her, and afterwards she stopped speaking almost entirely for about five years. A neighbour, Bertha Flowers, gave her books and asked her to read poems aloud. Slowly, through [[@shakespeare|Shakespeare]] and Black American poets, she found her [[@voice|voice]] again. She later said that this long silence taught her to listen, and to love the sound of words read aloud.

sec.h: A book that broke the silence
sec.t:
Her friend, the writer James Baldwin, encouraged her to write about her early life. *I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings* told the truth about racism and about the harm done to her as a child. It was honest about painful things, which was rare at the time.

Because of that honesty, it has often been challenged in American schools and libraries. Many teachers argue the opposite: that it helps readers who have suffered feel less alone. She went on to write six more books about her life, along with many books of poetry.

Her poem "Still I Rise" (1978) is about refusing to be kept down. It is read at school assemblies, protests and graduations around the world. She taught for many years at Wake Forest University in North Carolina, and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, America's highest award for a civilian, in 2011.

She died in 2014 at the age of 86. Her readings of her poems are still easy to find, and her deep, slow voice is part of why people remember them.
